label: 2 John 1:1–3
text:
"Elder" (presbyteros) can mean either an official governing title or simply "the old man" — John identifies himself with the plainest, least assuming word available, letting the letter's authority rest on its content rather than a claimed office.

"Elect lady" (eklektē kyria) is genuinely ambiguous in the Greek — kyria could be an ordinary title, "lady," a proper name, "Kyria," or a personification of a local congregation addressed as a single household; the letter's content, alternating singular and plural address, fits any of the three.

"Known" is egnōkosin, perfect tense — a knowledge of the truth already gained and, in the present, still fully possessed, not a partial or provisional acquaintance.

"Dwelleth" is menousan, present participle — the truth pictured as permanently, currently resident, the same continuous-abiding vocabulary John uses throughout his other letters.
translation: The elder, to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth — and not I only, but also all who have come to know the truth — because of the truth which is abiding in us, and will be with us forever: grace, mercy, peace will be with us, from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love.

label: 2 John 1:4–6
text:
"Rejoiced greatly" translates echarēn lian — lian is an intensifying adverb meaning "exceedingly," pushing an already strong verb further still.

"Walking in truth" is a present participle, peripatountas — an ongoing, habitual manner of life, not a single praiseworthy act singled out for mention.

The commandment described as simultaneously "new" and one "we had from the beginning" repeats, almost word for word, the identical paradox already worked through at length in 1 John 2:7-8 — old in origin, new in the fresh reality it takes on whenever it is actually lived.
translation: I rejoiced exceedingly that I have found some of your children walking in truth, just as we received commandment from the Father. And now I ask you, lady — not as writing a new commandment to you, but one which we have had from the beginning — that we should be loving one another. And this is love: that we should be walking according to his commandments. This is the commandment, just as you heard from the beginning, that you should be walking in it.

label: 2 John 1:7–11
text:
"Deceivers" is planoi, sharing a root with planē, "wandering, error" — the same word-family behind the modern "planet," a body that appears to stray from a fixed course.

"Transgresseth" translates proagōn, literally "going ahead, pressing forward beyond" — an ironic term for a false teacher who prides himself on progress, on advancing past settled teaching into something supposedly more refined, when in fact he has left the substance of the doctrine behind entirely.

"God speed" renders chairein, the ordinary Greek word of greeting, "rejoice, hail" — refusing even this common courtesy is a deliberate withholding of any gesture that could look like endorsement.

"Partaker" is koinōnei, present tense — the identical koinōnia root used throughout 1 John for genuine fellowship, here warning that even a simple greeting can function as active participation in another man's evil work.
translation: Because many deceivers have gone out into the world, those not confessing Jesus Christ coming in the flesh; this is the deceiver and the antichrist. Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose the things we have worked for, but that you receive a full reward. Everyone who goes ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ does not have God. The one who abides in the teaching, this one has both the Father and the Son. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, and do not say a greeting to him; for the one who says a greeting to him is sharing in his evil works.

label: 2 John 1:12–13
text:
"Paper and ink" translates chartou kai melanos — chartēs names a single sheet of papyrus, and melas, "black," stands in simply for the ink itself, a plain, physical description of the writing materials just set aside in favor of a promised visit.

"Face to face" is stoma pros stoma, literally "mouth to mouth" — a vivid Hebrew idiom for direct, unmediated conversation, preferred here over anything a letter, however carefully written, could accomplish.
translation: Having many things to write to you, I do not want to do so with paper and ink, but I am hoping to come to you and to speak mouth to mouth, so that our joy may be made full. The children of your elect sister greet you.
